fetched_contents.text: Understanding Lens Distortion In a previous post, we went over the geometry of image formation and learned how a point in 3D gets projected on to the image plane of a camera. The model we used was based on the pinhole camera model. The only time you use a pinhole camera is probably during an eclipse. The model of image formation for any real world camera involves a lens. Have you ever wondered why we attach a lens to our cameras? Does it affect the transformation defining the projection of a 3D points to a corresponding pixel in an image? If yes, how do we model it mathematically? In this post we will answer the above questions. Replacing the pinhole by a lens To generate clear and sharp images the diameter of the aperture (hole) of a pinhole camera should be as small as possible. If we increase the size of the aperture, we know that rays from multiple points of the object would be incident on the same part of the screen creating a blurred image. On the other hand, if we make the aperture size small, only a small number of photons hit the image sensor. As a result the image is dark and noisy. So, smaller the aperture of the pinhole camera, more focused is the image but, at the same time, darker and noisier it is. On the other hand, with a larger aperture, the image sensor receives more photons ( and hence more signal ). This leads to a bright image with only a small amount of noise. How do we get a sharp image but at the same time capture more light rays to make the image bright? We replace the pinhole by a lens thus increasing the size of the aperture through which light rays can pass. A lens allows larger number of rays to pass through the hole and because of its optical properties it can also focus them on the screen. This makes the image brighter. Awesome! So we have bright and sharp, focused image using a lens. The problem is solved? Right? Not so fast. fetched_contents.text: A Distortion Correction Method Based on Actual Camera Imaging Principles Abstract In the human–robot collaboration system, the high-precision distortion correction of the camera as an important sensor is a crucial prerequisite for accomplishing the task. The traditional correction process is to calculate the lens distortion with the camera model parameters or separately from the camera model. However, in the optimization process calculate with the camera model parameters, the mutual compensation between the parameters may lead to numerical instability, and the existing distortion correction methods separated from the camera model are difficult to ensure the accuracy of the correction. To address this problem, this study proposes a model-independent lens distortion correction method based on the image center area from the perspective of the actual camera lens distortion principle. The proposed method is based on the idea that the structured image preserves its ratios through perspective transformation, and uses the local image information in the central area of the image to correct the overall image. The experiments are verified from two cases of low distortion and high distortion under simulation and actual experiments. The experimental results show that the accuracy and stability of this method are better than other methods in training and testing results. Keywords: camera calibration, lens distortion correction, image restoration, model-independent method 1. Introduction In recent years, with the rapid development of computer vision and deep learning technology, cameras play an increasingly important role in human–robot collaboration sensing systems, especially in target detection and tracking and human motion recognition [1,2,3]. As a key technology of computer vision application, the accuracy and robustness of camera calibration directly affect the performance and reliability of robot sensing system [4]. The essence of camera calibration lies in establishing the mapping relationship between points in the scene and their corresponding points in the image, in which lens distortion is a problem that cannot be ignored. For instance, while the wide-angle camera can capture image data over a broad field of view, they are susceptible to issues such as significant deformation of edge pixels and serious information distortion. Therefore, in order to ensure the accuracy of subsequent algorithms, it is essential to correct the camera distortion. Based on distinct calibration approaches, the camera calibration methods are typically classified into three categories: camera self-calibration method, active vision-based calibration method, and template-based calibration method. The camera self-calibration method utilizes the correspondence of the surroundings under multiple viewpoints during the camera’s natural motion to calibrate the reference target independently. Faugeras [5] and Maybank et al. [6] proposed a method based on Kruppa’s equation to solve the camera parameters directly. Liu [7] proposed a linear self-calibration method for projection cameras based on the representing of deforming object by the trajectory basis. The camera self-calibration method is excellently flexible, but has low accuracy, low robustness, and requires solving nonlinear equations. The camera parameters are determined through precise camera movement control in the active vision-based calibration method. De Ma [8] proposed a linear calibration method based on two sets of three orthogonal motions. Hartley [9] proposed a calibration method based on the pure rotational motion of the camera optical center. The active vision-based calibration method is simple and robust, but it has a high system cost, and is not applicable when the camera motion parameters are unknown or the camera motion cannot be precisely controlled. The template-based calibration method utilizes the known scene structure information to achieve camera calibration. Tsai [10] utilized a two-step calibration technique to achieve efficient calibration of the camera’s external position and attitude. Weng [11] and Gao [12] further investigated the two-step calibration. The method utilizes the metric information of three-dimensional [13], two-dimensional [14,15], or one-dimensional [16] templates to solve the camera model parameters with high calibration accuracy and robustness. Compared with the previous two methods, the template-based calibration method has wide applicability and provides more possibilities to solve the camera calibration problems in various practical applications. Taking into account the aforementioned factors, a template-based correction method was used in this study. Currently, the most widely used camera calibration toolboxes [17,18] of the template-based calibration method are constructed based on Zhang’s technique [14] by capturing chessboard corner points. Heikkila [15] and Chen et al. [19] calibrated the camera by quadratic curve fitting based on circular array images without calculating the center of the circle. The above methods are based on the recognition results through iterative optimization to estimate the camera parameters and distortion coefficients simultaneously. However, this process leads to unstable parameter results due to the mutual compensation between parameters to reach the optimal solution. The analysis above indicates the need to correct the distortion individually and to obtain accurate camera parameters by correcting the control points. Practical estimation and calibration methods for lens distortion are centered around estimating intrinsic camera parameters, especially distortion coefficients, from image data. The most common calibration methods are template-based, active vision-based, and self-calibration methods. Template-based methods use known scene structure, such as chessboard corners, circular arrays, or other structured patterns, to estimate both camera parameters and distortion coefficients simultaneously [N3-F2]. Active vision-based methods use controlled camera motion to calibrate the system, while self-calibration methods rely on natural motion and scene structure without precise control over the camera’s movement [N3-F2]. In practice, calibration often focuses on estimating radial distortion coefficients (K₁, K₂, K₃) and tangential distortion coefficients (P₁, P₂), which are returned by methods like OpenCV’s `calibrateCamera` [N1-F1].

Parameters are optimized from image data through iterative optimization or closed-form solutions. Template-based calibration typically uses iterative algorithms to minimize the residual error between observed image points and their inferred projections computed with the estimated calibration parameters [N5-F3]. The optimization objective is often the mean-square discrepancy between observed image points and their inferred image projections, and the procedure may improve initial estimates iteratively through nonlinear optimization [N5-F3]. Some methods also use closed-form solutions in the first step before refining them with nonlinear optimization [N5-F3]. This approach is useful because it reduces the risk of getting stuck in a poor local minimum, especially when distortion parameters are included in the parameter space [N5-F3].

Common assumptions or constraints made during calibration include that the camera model is sufficiently general to cover the dominant distortion types, that the scene structure is known or can be modeled, and that the camera’s intrinsic and extrinsic parameters are consistent with the distortion model [N5-F3]. In practice, calibration also assumes that the image plane is approximately flat and that the sensor or image screen is at a known position relative to the optical axis [N1-F1]. The MathWorks description notes that tangential distortion occurs when the lens and image plane are not parallel, and that the tangential distortion coefficients model this type of distortion [N2-R2]. These assumptions make the calibration process more tractable but also mean that more complex models may be needed when the camera’s internal misalignment is substantial [N5-F3].

In context, distortion calibration is important for applications such as wide-angle image correction, panorama stitching, and real-time image processing, where undistorted coordinates are needed for accurate rectification or stitching [N4-R1][N4-R3][N4-R5]. The evidence also indicates that calibration is often used in precision optical measurement systems, where even small distortion errors can affect quantitative measurements [N3-R3]. Overall, practical calibration balances accuracy, robustness, and computational simplicity by using structured patterns, iterative optimization, and assumptions about scene geometry and camera alignment [N3-F2][N5-F3].

In real-world practice, the main distortion categories most commonly distinguished are radial distortion, tangential distortion, decentering distortion, and thin prism distortion [N1-R1][N5-R1][N5-F3]. These categories are not mutually exclusive: radial distortion includes barrel and pincushion effects, and decentering and thin prism distortions have both radial and tangential components [N1-F1][N5-F3]. The distinction is important because each type of distortion arises from a different physical mechanism.

Barrel distortion and pincushion distortion are the two classic radial distortion effects. Barrel distortion occurs when light rays bend more near the edges of the lens than near the center, causing straight lines to appear bowed outward from the center [N1-R2][N1-F1]. Pincushion distortion is the opposite: light rays bend more near the center, causing straight lines to appear bowed inward toward the center [N1-R2][N1-F1]. Radial distortion is usually caused by unequal bending of light rays across the lens [N1-F1]. In practice, radial distortion is the most commonly distinguished category because it is the dominant source of distortion in many cameras and is well modeled by distortion coefficients such as K₁, K₂, K₃ [N1-F1][N5-F3].

Tangential distortion occurs when the image screen or sensor is at an angle relative to the lens, causing the image to appear tilted or stretched [N1-F1][N2-R2]. The MathWorks description explicitly states that tangential distortion occurs when the lens and image plane are not parallel, and that the tangential distortion coefficients model this type of distortion [N2-R2]. Physically, tangential distortion arises from misalignment between the optical axis and the image sensor, rather than from uneven bending of light rays across the lens [N1-F1].

Decentering distortion and thin prism distortion are specialized categories that extend beyond basic radial/tangential models. Decentering distortion arises when the optical center of the lens is not aligned with the image sensor, while thin prism distortion occurs when a thin prism-like effect causes image displacement [N1-F1][N5-F3]. The academic source explicitly states that the camera model accounts for major sources of camera distortion, including radial, decentering, and thin prism distortions [N5-F3]. In practice, these more complex distortion types are usually included in calibration when the camera’s internal misalignment is substantial or when high accuracy is required [N5-F3].

Overall, distortion is classified as radial, tangential, or both. Radial distortion includes barrel and pincushion effects, and decentering and thin prism distortions also have radial and tangential components [N1-F1][N5-F3]. This means that the simplest practical classification is radial distortion plus tangential distortion, but more sophisticated models distinguish additional sources of distortion when higher accuracy is needed [N1-F1][N5-F3].

The most commonly used practical model is the radial/tangential model, which is simple enough for many applications yet powerful enough to capture the dominant sources of distortion [N1-F1][N5-F3]. However, more complex models are used when the camera’s internal misalignment is substantial, when high accuracy is required, or when specialized distortion sources must be addressed [N5-F3]. The evidence shows that calibration models can be classified into direct nonlinear minimization and closed-form solutions, with nonlinear optimization often used to refine initial estimates [N5-F3].

In different applications, different models are preferred. Template-based calibration is widely used because it provides wide applicability and robustness, especially for precision optical measurement systems and computer vision applications [N3-F2][N5-F3]. Active vision-based methods are preferred when camera motion can be precisely controlled, because they are simple and robust, but they are not always practical when motion parameters are unknown or the camera cannot be controlled precisely [N3-F2]. Self-calibration methods are preferred when natural scene motion is available, but they tend to be less accurate and less robust than template-based methods [N3-F2]. For applications requiring very high accuracy, such as close-range photogrammetry and quantitative measurements, models that include decentering and thin prism distortion are preferred because they account for more of the camera’s internal misalignment [N5-F3].

Model complexity affects accuracy and robustness in a clear way: more complex models can better capture the true distortion behavior, especially when the camera has significant decentering or thin prism effects [N5-F3]. However, increased complexity also makes optimization more difficult and can reduce robustness if the initial guess is poor or if the optimization procedure is not well designed [N5-F3]. The evidence notes that once distortion parameters are included in the parameter space, minimization may become unstable if the iteration procedure is not properly designed, and that interactions between distortion parameters and external parameters can lead to divergence or false solutions [N5-F3]. Therefore, the preferred choice is usually a balance between sufficient complexity and numerical stability.

Radial/tangential models are preferred when the main distortion is radial and when the system can tolerate a simpler model [N1-F1][N5-F3]. Decentering/thin prism models are preferred when the camera has substantial internal misalignment, such as when the CCD sensing array is not orthogonal to the optical axis or the center of the array does not coincide with the optical principal point [N5-F3]. The Brown distortion model is also a key practical choice because it explicitly separates radial and tangential distortion and is widely used in calibration toolboxes [N6-R1][N6-R4]. Overall, the evidence supports the conclusion that practical calibration model choices are application-driven, with more complex models used when higher accuracy is needed and simpler models used when robustness and computational simplicity are more important [N3-F2][N5-F3][N6-R1].

The optimization objective is often the **mean-square discrepancy** between observed image points and their inferred image projections, and the procedure may improve initial estimates iteratively through nonlinear optimization [N5-F3]. ## Which distortion models are used in different applications

Calibration model choices are determined by the trade-off between **accuracy**, **robustness**, and **computational complexity**. The most commonly used practical model is the **radial/tangential model**, which is simple enough for many applications yet powerful enough to capture the dominant sources of distortion [N1-F1][N5-F3]. However, more complex models are used when the camera’s internal misalignment is substantial, when high accuracy is required, or when specialized distortion sources must be addressed [N5-F3].

In different applications, different models are preferred. **Template-based calibration** is widely used because it provides wide applicability and robustness, especially for precision optical measurement systems and computer vision applications [N3-F2][N5-F3]. **Active vision-based methods** are preferred when camera motion can be precisely controlled, because they are simple and robust, but they are not always practical when motion parameters are unknown or the camera cannot be controlled precisely [N3-F2]. **Self-calibration methods** are preferred when natural scene motion is available, but they tend to be less accurate and less robust than template-based methods [N3-F2]. For applications requiring very high accuracy, such as close-range photogrammetry and quantitative measurements, models that include **decentering** and **thin prism distortion** are preferred because they account for more of the camera’s internal misalignment [N5-F3].

## How model complexity affects accuracy and robustness

Model complexity affects accuracy and robustness in a clear way: more complex models can better capture the true distortion behavior, especially when the camera has significant decentering or thin prism effects [N5-F3]. However, increased complexity also makes optimization more difficult and can reduce robustness if the initial guess is poor or if the optimization procedure is not well designed [N5-F3]. The evidence notes that once distortion parameters are included in the parameter space, minimization may become unstable if the iteration procedure is not properly designed, and that interactions between distortion parameters and external parameters can lead to divergence or false solutions [N5-F3]. Therefore, the preferred choice is usually a balance between sufficient complexity and numerical stability.

## When radial/tangential/decentering/thin prism models are preferred

Radial/tangential models are preferred when the main distortion is radial and when the system can tolerate a simpler model [N1-F1][N5-F3]. Decentering/thin prism models are preferred when the camera has substantial internal misalignment, such as when the CCD sensing array is not orthogonal to the optical axis or the center of the array does not coincide with the optical principal point [N5-F3]. The **Brown distortion model** is also a key practical choice because it explicitly separates radial and tangential distortion and is widely used in calibration toolboxes [N6-R1][N6-R4].

## Conclusion

In summary, the main types of real-world lens distortions are **radial distortion**, **tangential distortion**, **decentering distortion**, and **thin prism distortion** [N1-R1][N5-R1][N5-F3]. These are typically parameterized using a combination of **radial coefficients** (K₁, K₂, K₃) and **tangential coefficients** (P₁, P₂), with more complex models adding decentering and thin prism terms when needed [N1-F1][N5-F3]. Distortion is estimated and calibrated through template-based, active vision-based, or self-calibration methods, with parameters optimized via iterative optimization or closed-form refinement [N3-F2][N5-F3]. Model complexity is preferred when accuracy matters, but practical choices are usually guided by the trade-off between accuracy, robustness, and computational simplicity [N1-F1][N5-F3][N6-R1].
